cards.q: A servo drive has current, speed and position loops, one inside the other. Which is tuned first?
options: The innermost, the current (torque) loop, then speed, then position
The position loop, then speed, then current
All three at once
Only the position loop needs tuning
cards.why: Each outer loop relies on the one inside it. Tune from the inside out; the current loop is often set automatically from the motor data.

cards.q: The speed loop's proportional gain is raised too far. What do you expect?
options: Oscillation: the axis rings, hunts or whines, and may go unstable
The axis gets slower to respond
Nothing: more gain is always better
The motor loses torque
cards.why: More gain responds harder to error, up to a point; beyond it the loop overshoots each correction and oscillates. You hear it before you see it.

cards.q: Why must each inner loop respond several times faster than the loop around it?
options: So the outer loop sees the inner one as near-instant; if they are close in speed they fight and oscillate
So that the inner loop uses less current
Because the outer loop is always digital
It does not matter which is faster
cards.why: The outer loop's tuning assumes its command is carried out at once. A rule of thumb is three to ten times the bandwidth for each loop inwards.

cards.q: What does velocity feedforward do in a position loop?
options: Adds the commanded speed straight to the speed command, so the loop need not build up a following error to make the axis move
Measures the speed more accurately
Slows the axis near the target
Replaces the encoder
cards.why: Without it, only a position error can produce a speed command, so the axis always lags. Feedforward supplies the speed it already knows it needs; feedback corrects the rest.

cards.q: An axis's inertia at the motor is {j} kg·m². The profile commands an acceleration of {a} rad/s². What feedforward torque does that need, in N·m?
cards.why: Torque to accelerate an inertia: $T = J\alpha$. Acceleration feedforward adds that torque as the profile accelerates, before any error appears.

cards.q: Why can feedforward not position an axis on its own?
options: It is open loop: it cannot correct for friction, load changes or a wrong inertia figure, so feedback is still needed
It makes the axis too slow
It only works on stepper motors
It needs the axis to be stationary
cards.why: Feedforward acts on what it expects; feedback acts on what actually happened. Together, feedforward does most of the work and feedback trims the error.

cards.q: A motor runs at {n} rpm into a {r}:1 gearbox. How fast does the output shaft turn, in rpm?
cards.why: A reduction of {r}:1 divides the speed by {r} (and multiplies the torque by about as much).

cards.q: A motor gives {t} N·m into a {r}:1 gearbox that is {e}% efficient. What torque comes out, in N·m?
cards.why: Torque multiplies by the ratio, less the losses: $T_{out} = T_{in} \times r \times \eta$.

cards.q: How does an electronic cam differ from electronic gearing?
options: The slave's position follows a profile of the master's position, so the ratio changes through the cycle; gearing keeps one fixed ratio
A cam is always mechanical
Gearing needs no master axis
A cam runs the slave at constant speed
cards.why: Electronic gearing: slave = ratio × master, all the way round. A cam table maps each master position to a slave position, as a mechanical cam's shape would.

cards.q: Why does an axis with an incremental encoder need homing after power-up?
options: An incremental encoder only counts movement, so at power-up the drive does not know where the axis is
To warm up the motor
To test the brake
Absolute encoders need it, incremental ones do not
cards.why: Incremental means counting pulses from wherever it started. Homing gives the count a known starting point. An absolute encoder knows its position at power-up.

cards.q: A homing sequence finds the home switch at speed. What does a good sequence do next, for accuracy?
options: Moves slowly to the switch's edge, or on to the encoder's marker (index) pulse, and takes that as home
Stops wherever it is and calls that home
Runs back to the other end of travel
Nothing: a switch is accurate at any speed
cards.why: A switch found at speed is found late, and by different amounts each time. Creeping to its edge, or to the once-a-revolution marker pulse, repeats to a fraction of a millimetre.

cards.q: An axis has software limits and hard limit switches. How should they be set?
options: Software limits inside the travel; hard limits a little beyond them, as the last line if the position or software is wrong
Hard limits inside the software limits
Either one is enough
Both at exactly the same place
cards.why: Software limits stop normal moves at the edge of the working range. The hard limits must only ever be reached when something has gone wrong, such as a lost home. Mechanical end stops lie beyond both.

cards.q: A load's inertia is {j} kg·m². It is driven through a {r}:1 gearbox. What inertia does the motor see?
cards.why: Inertia reflects through a gearbox by the ratio **squared**: $J_{motor} = \frac{J_{load}}{r^2}$.

cards.q: Why do servo sizing guides suggest keeping the load-to-motor inertia ratio low, such as 10:1 or less (lower still for very fast moves)?
options: With a large ratio the load dominates, and any springiness in the drive train makes the loop hard to tune and prone to resonance
The motor runs hotter with a small load
A high ratio makes the motor faster
It is only about cost
cards.why: The motor has to control the load through couplings and belts that twist a little. The heavier the load compared with the rotor, the more that twisting shows up as ringing.

cards.q: A load's inertia is {jl} kg·m² and the motor's rotor {jm} kg·m². What gear ratio makes the reflected load inertia equal the rotor's?
cards.why: Set $\frac{J_L}{r^2} = J_M$, so $r = \sqrt{\frac{J_L}{J_M}}$.

cards.q: A variable-speed drive brings a heavy flywheel to a stop quickly. Where does the flywheel's energy go?
options: Back into the drive's DC bus as the motor acts as a generator; a brake resistor burns it off, or a regenerative unit returns it to the supply
It is stored in the motor
Into the mains automatically, with every drive
It disappears as the speed falls
cards.why: Slowing a load means the load drives the motor. The bus voltage rises; without a brake resistor or regeneration the drive trips on overvoltage.

cards.q: A load of inertia {j} kg·m² spins at {n} rpm. How much kinetic energy does it hold, in kJ?
cards.why: $E = \tfrac{1}{2}J\omega^2$ with $\omega$ in rad/s: rpm × $2\pi$ ÷ 60.

cards.q: Each machine cycle dumps {e} kJ into a brake resistor, and a cycle lasts {t} s. What average power must the resistor take, in watts?
cards.why: Average power = energy ÷ time. The resistor must also take the peak power while braking, which is much higher.

cards.q: Before changing a drive's parameters, what should you do first?
options: Save a copy of the parameter set as it is, so you can put it back
Reset the drive to factory settings
Change the motor data
Nothing: changes can always be undone on the keypad
cards.why: A backup is the one sure way back. Factory reset throws away the motor data and every setting the machine relies on.

cards.q: A drive trips on overcurrent only while accelerating a heavy load. What is the likely cause?
options: The acceleration ramp is too short for the load's inertia (or the boost is too high)
The deceleration ramp is too short
The motor is too big
The encoder is dirty
cards.why: Accelerating a large inertia quickly needs a lot of torque, so a lot of current. Lengthen the ramp, or check the boost and the motor data.

cards.q: A drive trips on DC bus overvoltage only while slowing down. What is the likely cause and cure?
options: The load's energy is coming back faster than the drive can get rid of it: lengthen the deceleration ramp, or fit and enable a correctly sized brake resistor
The mains voltage is too low
The acceleration ramp is too long
The motor cable is too long
cards.why: Regenerated energy charges the bus capacitors. Slower deceleration returns it more gently; a brake chopper and resistor burn it off.
